claim: Genome-wide association studies have implicated common genomic variants in the gene desert upstream of TBX3 in cardiac conduction velocity.
source: Genome-wide association studies have implicated common genomic variants in the gene desert upstream of TBX3 in cardiac conduction velocity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to GWAS studies throughout the manuscript.

claim: The entire 1.3 Mb human and mouse TBX3 locus was tested for regulatory function using high-throughput STARR-seq.
source: Here, we use high-throughput STARR-seq to test the entire 1.3 Mb human and mouse TBX3 locus, including two cardiac conduction-associated variant regions, for regulatory function.
evidence: The methods describe the STARR-seq procedure and the manuscript presents data from these experiments.

claim: Multiple accessible and functional regulatory DNA elements that harbor variants affecting their activity were identified.
source: We identified multiple accessible and functional regulatory DNA elements that harbor variants affecting their activity.
evidence: This is supported by STARR-seq data, ATAC-seq data, and luciferase assays presented in the results.

claim: Both variant regions drove gene expression in the cardiac conduction tissue in transgenic reporter mice.
source: Both variant regions drove gene expression in the cardiac conduction tissue in transgenic reporter mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by BAC transgenic reporter experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Genomic deletion of one of the variant regions from the mouse genome caused increased cardiac expression of only Tbx3.
source: Genomic deletion from the mouse genome of one of the regions caused increased cardiac expression of only Tbx3, PR interval shortening and increased QRS duration.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from Tbx3ΔVR2/ΔVR2 mice shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: Genomic deletion of one of the variant regions caused PR interval shortening.
source: Genomic deletion from the mouse genome of one of the regions caused increased cardiac expression of only Tbx3, PR interval shortening and increased QRS duration.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ECG measurements in Tbx3ΔVR2/ΔVR2 mice shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Genomic deletion of one of the variant regions caused increased QRS duration.
source: Genomic deletion from the mouse genome of one of the regions caused increased cardiac expression of only Tbx3, PR interval shortening and increased QRS duration.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ECG measurements in Tbx3ΔVR2/ΔVR2 mice shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The majority of trait-associated genetic variants is found in noncoding genomic DNA.
source: The majority of trait-associated genetic variants (single nucleotide polymorphisms; SNPs) is found in noncoding genomic DNA, and is thought to affect the function of cis-regulatory elements (REs) controlling the activity of their target gene promoters (Deplancke et al., 2016; Maurano et al., 2012; Schaub et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Noncoding variants are thought to affect the function of cis-regulatory elements controlling target gene promoters.
source: The majority of trait-associated genetic variants (single nucleotide polymorphisms; SNPs) is found in noncoding genomic DNA, and is thought to affect the function of cis-regulatory elements (REs) controlling the activity of their target gene promoters (Deplancke et al., 2016; Maurano et al., 2012; Schaub et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Common variation can lead to both down- and upregulation of target gene expression.
source: Expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) analyses show that common variation can lead to both down- and upregulation of target gene expression (Gutierrez and Chung, 2016; Hsu et al., 2018; Roselli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to eQTL studies.

claim: The atrioventricular conduction system conducts the electrical impulse from atria to ventricles and synchronizes ventricular activation.
source: The atrioventricular conduction system (AVCS) conducts the electrical impulse from atria to ventricles and synchronizes ventricular activation, thus orchestrating the rhythm of the heart.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cardiac physiology.

claim: Disrupted AVCS function can lead to life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias and hypertrophy.
source: Disrupted AVCS function can lead to life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias and hypertrophy (Aeschbacher et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Common SNPs in the gene desert upstream of TBX3 have been strongly associated with both PR interval and QRS duration.
source: Common SNPs in the gene desert upstream of TBX3 have been strongly associated with both PR interval and QRS duration (Pfeufer et al., 2010; Sotoodehnia et al., 2010; van der Harst et al., 2016; van Setten et al., 2018; Verweij et al., 2014), ECG parameters directly reflective of AVCS function and representing the time between the first moment of activation of the atria and the ventricles, and ventricular activation, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by multiple GWAS citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PR interval and QRS duration are ECG parameters directly reflective of AVCS function.
source: Common SNPs in the gene desert upstream of TBX3 have been strongly associated with both PR interval and QRS duration (Pfeufer et al., 2010; Sotoodehnia et al., 2010; van der Harst et al., 2016; van Setten et al., 2018; Verweij et al., 2014), ECG parameters directly reflective of AVCS function and representing the time between the first moment of activation of the atria and the ventricles, and ventricular activation, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ECG parameters.

claim: Tbx3 is specifically expressed in the AVCS, including the AV node, AV bundle and proximal bundle branches.
source: The T-box transcription factor 3 (Tbx3) is specifically expressed in the AVCS, including the AV node, AV bundle and proximal bundle branches, and plays a critical role in its development and function (Bakker et al., 2012; Bakker et al., 2008; Frank et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tbx3 plays a critical role in AVCS development and function.
source: The T-box transcription factor 3 (Tbx3) is specifically expressed in the AVCS, including the AV node, AV bundle and proximal bundle branches, and plays a critical role in its development and function (Bakker et al., 2012; Bakker et al., 2008; Frank et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TBX5 plays a key role in AVCS development and function.
source: Presumably, the SNPs upstream of TBX3 affect the expression of TBX3 or other nearby genes, such as TBX5, which also plays a key role in AVCS development and function (Arnolds et al., 2012; Burnicka-Turek et al., 2020), or MED13L, encoding a subunit of the ubiquitously expressed Mediator complex involved in transcriptional activation (Asadollahi et al., 2013; van Haelst et al., 2015) and recently implicated in heart rate recovery after exercise (Ramírez et al., 2018; Verweij et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MED13L encodes a subunit of the ubiquitously expressed Mediator complex involved in transcriptional activation.
source: Presumably, the SNPs upstream of TBX3 affect the expression of TBX3 or other nearby genes, such as TBX5, which also plays a key role in AVCS development and function (Arnolds et al., 2012; Burnicka-Turek et al., 2020), or MED13L, encoding a subunit of the ubiquitously expressed Mediator complex involved in transcriptional activation (Asadollahi et al., 2013; van Haelst et al., 2015) and recently implicated in heart rate recovery after exercise (Ramírez et al., 2018; Verweij et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MED13L has been recently implicated in heart rate recovery after exercise.
source: Presumably, the SNPs upstream of TBX3 affect the expression of TBX3 or other nearby genes, such as TBX5, which also plays a key role in AVCS development and function (Arnolds et al., 2012; Burnicka-Turek et al., 2020), or MED13L, encoding a subunit of the ubiquitously expressed Mediator complex involved in transcriptional activation (Asadollahi et al., 2013; van Haelst et al., 2015) and recently implicated in heart rate recovery after exercise (Ramírez et al., 2018; Verweij et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The availability of relevant cells for functional and epigenomic experiments is hampered by the very small proportion of TBX3+ AVCS cardiomyocytes in the heart.
source: Efforts to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the transcriptional regulation of AVCS genes and the role of genetic variation are challenging, as the availability of relevant cells for functional and (epi)genomic experiments is hampered by the very small proportion of TBX3+ AVCS cardiomyocytes in the heart and the heterogeneous cellular composition of the AVCS (Aanhaanen et al., 2010; Hoogaars et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing AVCS composition.

claim: The AVCS has a heterogeneous cellular composition.
source: Efforts to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the transcriptional regulation of AVCS genes and the role of genetic variation are challenging, as the availability of relevant cells for functional and (epi)genomic experiments is hampered by the very small proportion of TBX3+ AVCS cardiomyocytes in the heart and the heterogeneous cellular composition of the AVCS (Aanhaanen et al., 2010; Hoogaars et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: eQTL data for TBX3 in cardiac tissue is not available.
source: Along this line, eQTL data for TBX3 in cardiac tissue is not available, and AVCS tissue from human hearts is not expected to become available soon.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in the manuscript.

claim: Suitable AVCS-like cell lines do not exist.
source: Moreover, suitable AVCS-like cell lines, derived from stem cells or immortalized primary cells do not exist.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in the manuscript.

claim: Current cardiac epigenomic datasets from humans are mainly derived from whole heart or heart compartment tissue.
source: Current cardiac epigenomic datasets from humans are mainly derived from whole heart or heart compartment tissue and are not suitable for the identification of AVCS REs, as the proportion of AVCS cells in these tissues is extremely small.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in the manuscript.

claim: Current cardiac epigenomic datasets are not suitable for the identification of AVCS REs because the proportion of AVCS cells in these tissues is extremely small.
source: Current cardiac epigenomic datasets from humans are mainly derived from whole heart or heart compartment tissue and are not suitable for the identification of AVCS REs, as the proportion of AVCS cells in these tissues is extremely small.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation and justification for the study approach.

claim: TBX3 and its upstream gene desert are organized in a TAD of approximately 1.3 Mb.
source: TBX3 and its upstream gene desert are organized in a TAD of approximately 1.3 Mb that is delimited by binding sites for CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF; a zinc-finger protein associated with enhancer-promoter looping and TAD boundary formation [de Wit et al., 2015; Nora et al., 2017]) and physically separated from that of the neighboring gene MED13L, corresponding to the organization of the murine loci in cardiac embryonic tissue (van Weerd et al., 2014; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 1A and citations.

claim: The TBX3 TAD is delimited by binding sites for CTCF.
source: TBX3 and its upstream gene desert are organized in a TAD of approximately 1.3 Mb that is delimited by binding sites for CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF; a zinc-finger protein associated with enhancer-promoter looping and TAD boundary formation [de Wit et al., 2015; Nora et al., 2017]) and physically separated from that of the neighboring gene MED13L, corresponding to the organization of the murine loci in cardiac embryonic tissue (van Weerd et al., 2014; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A with CTCF ChIP-seq data and supported by citations.

claim: CTCF is a zinc-finger protein associated with enhancer-promoter looping and TAD boundary formation.
source: TBX3 and its upstream gene desert are organized in a TAD of approximately 1.3 Mb that is delimited by binding sites for CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF; a zinc-finger protein associated with enhancer-promoter looping and TAD boundary formation [de Wit et al., 2015; Nora et al., 2017]) and physically separated from that of the neighboring gene MED13L, corresponding to the organization of the murine loci in cardiac embryonic tissue (van Weerd et al., 2014; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The TBX3 TAD is physically separated from that of the neighboring gene MED13L.
source: TBX3 and its upstream gene desert are organized in a TAD of approximately 1.3 Mb that is delimited by binding sites for CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF; a zinc-finger protein associated with enhancer-promoter looping and TAD boundary formation [de Wit et al., 2015; Nora et al., 2017]) and physically separated from that of the neighboring gene MED13L, corresponding to the organization of the murine loci in cardiac embryonic tissue (van Weerd et al., 2014; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A with Hi-C data.

claim: Sequences within the TADs of TBX3 and TBX5 physically interact with each other to some extent.
source: Sequences within the TADs of TBX3 and TBX5 physically interact with each other to some extent.
evidence: This is inferred from the Hi-C data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Variants associated with both PR interval and QRS duration are located in a region approximately −261 kb to −221 kb upstream of TBX3 (VR1).
source: Variants associated with both PR interval (van Setten et al., 2018) and QRS duration (van der Harst et al., 2016) are located in a region approximately −261 kb to −221 kb upstream of TBX3 (variant region (VR) 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and supported by citations to GWAS studies.

claim: A second region (VR2) ranging from −85 kb to −6 kb upstream of TBX3 harbors SNPs associated with only PR interval.
source: A second region (VR2) ranging from −85 kb to −6 kb upstream of TBX3 harbors SNPs associated with only PR interval.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and supported by GWAS data.

claim: SNPs associated with QRS duration were found downstream of TBX3.
source: SNPs associated with QRS duration were also found downstream of TBX3.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 67 genomic regions within the Tbx3/Tbx5 regulatory domain are accessible in AVCS cardiomyocytes.
source: 67 genomic regions within the Tbx3/Tbx5 regulatory domain, as determined by chromatin conformation capture (van Weerd et al., 2014), are accessible in AVCS cardiomyocytes, including the previously identified AV canal enhancers Tbx3-eA and Tbx3-eB (van Weerd et al., 2014; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The previously identified AV canal enhancers Tbx3-eA and Tbx3-eB are accessible in AVCS cardiomyocytes.
source: 67 genomic regions within the Tbx3/Tbx5 regulatory domain, as determined by chromatin conformation capture (van Weerd et al., 2014), are accessible in AVCS cardiomyocytes, including the previously identified AV canal enhancers Tbx3-eA and Tbx3-eB (van Weerd et al., 2014; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 1B and citations to previous work.

claim: Binding motifs for Smad2-4 and Gata4/6 are enriched in AVCS-specific accessible sequences.
source: Interestingly, AVCS-specific accessible sequences were enriched for motifs for members of the Smad and Gata families of transcription factors (Smad2-4, Gata4/6), involved in the activation of regulatory sequences (including Tbx3-eA) specifically in the AV canal (Stefanovic et al., 2014), and for Tcf factors (Tcf4, Tcf3) acting downstream of canonical Wnt-signaling to regulate AV canal specification (Gillers et al., 2015; Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1-Supplementary Table 1).
evidence: This is based on HOMER motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Smad and Gata family transcription factors are involved in the activation of regulatory sequences specifically in the AV canal.
source: Interestingly, AVCS-specific accessible sequences were enriched for motifs for members of the Smad and Gata families of transcription factors (Smad2-4, Gata4/6), involved in the activation of regulatory sequences (including Tbx3-eA) specifically in the AV canal (Stefanovic et al., 2014), and for Tcf factors (Tcf4, Tcf3) acting downstream of canonical Wnt-signaling to regulate AV canal specification (Gillers et al., 2015; Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1-Supplementary Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Binding motifs for Tcf factors are enriched in AVCS-specific accessible sequences.
source: Interestingly, AVCS-specific accessible sequences were enriched for motifs for members of the Smad and Gata families of transcription factors (Smad2-4, Gata4/6), involved in the activation of regulatory sequences (including Tbx3-eA) specifically in the AV canal (Stefanovic et al., 2014), and for Tcf factors (Tcf4, Tcf3) acting downstream of canonical Wnt-signaling to regulate AV canal specification (Gillers et al., 2015; Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1-Supplementary Table 1).
evidence: This is based on HOMER motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Tcf factors act downstream of canonical Wnt-signaling to regulate AV canal specification.
source: Interestingly, AVCS-specific accessible sequences were enriched for motifs for members of the Smad and Gata families of transcription factors (Smad2-4, Gata4/6), involved in the activation of regulatory sequences (including Tbx3-eA) specifically in the AV canal (Stefanovic et al., 2014), and for Tcf factors (Tcf4, Tcf3) acting downstream of canonical Wnt-signaling to regulate AV canal specification (Gillers et al., 2015; Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1-Supplementary Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: 28 of the 67 AVCS regions overlapped with accessible ventricular regions.
source: Of the 67 AVCS regions, 28 overlapped with accessible ventricular regions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 216 SG4-responsive regions were found in the murine locus.
source: Combined, we found 216 SG4- and 257 Wnt-responsive regions in the murine locus, and 206 SG4- and 190 Wnt-responsive regions in the human locus (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on STARR-seq data analysis.

claim: 257 Wnt-responsive regions were found in the murine locus.
source: Combined, we found 216 SG4- and 257 Wnt-responsive regions in the murine locus, and 206 SG4- and 190 Wnt-responsive regions in the human locus (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on STARR-seq data analysis.

claim: 206 SG4-responsive regions were found in the human locus.
source: Combined, we found 216 SG4- and 257 Wnt-responsive regions in the murine locus, and 206 SG4- and 190 Wnt-responsive regions in the human locus (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on STARR-seq data analysis.

claim: 190 Wnt-responsive regions were found in the human locus.
source: Combined, we found 216 SG4- and 257 Wnt-responsive regions in the murine locus, and 206 SG4- and 190 Wnt-responsive regions in the human locus (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on STARR-seq data analysis.

claim: Approximately 20% of the active mSTARR regions for both SG4- and Wnt-stimulation were functionally conserved between mouse and human.
source: The transcriptional potential of approximately 20% of the active mSTARR regions for both SG4- and Wnt-stimulation was functionally conserved between mouse and human, as the human homologues of these regions were active in the respective human STARR-seq libraries as well (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: 84% of m/hSTARR regions (n = 19) drove luciferase activity >2 fold relative to the vector containing only the core promoter.
source: 84% of m/hSTARR regions (n = 19) drove luciferase activity >2 fold relative to the vector containing only the core promoter, compared to 10% of randomly selected negative regions (n = 10; m/hSTARR fold change <1.5; p=0.0007 (two-sample t-test)) (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is based on luciferase assay validation shown in Figure 2G.

claim: 10% of randomly selected negative regions (n = 10) drove luciferase activity >2 fold relative to the vector containing only the core promoter.
source: 84% of m/hSTARR regions (n = 19) drove luciferase activity >2 fold relative to the vector containing only the core promoter, compared to 10% of randomly selected negative regions (n = 10; m/hSTARR fold change <1.5; p=0.0007 (two-sample t-test)) (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is based on luciferase assay validation shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The difference in luciferase activity between STARR-positive and negative regions is statistically significant (p=0.0007).
source: 84% of m/hSTARR regions (n = 19) drove luciferase activity >2 fold relative to the vector containing only the core promoter, compared to 10% of randomly selected negative regions (n = 10; m/hSTARR fold change <1.5; p=0.0007 (two-sample t-test)) (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of luciferase assay data.

claim: Both human and murine homologues of Tbx3-eA and Tbx3-eB are among the active regions identified by STARR-seq.
source: Among the active regions are both human and murine homologues of Tbx3-eA and Tbx3-eB.
evidence: This validates the STARR-seq approach by identifying known enhancers.

claim: The 216 mSTARR_SG4 sequences were enriched for binding motifs for Smad and Gata factors when compared to mSTARR_Wnt active sequences.
source: To further justify the legitimacy of the chosen >1.5 threshold for fold activity and to validate that the identified regions were indeed activated by either SG4- or Wnt-factors, we performed transcription factor motif enrichment analysis and found that the 216 mSTARR_SG4 sequences were enriched for binding motifs for Smad and Gata factors when compared to an equal number of randomly selected mSTARR_Wnt active sequences.
evidence: This is based on HOMER motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Binding motifs for Tcf factors are enriched in the 257 mSTARR_Wnt regions when compared to mSTARR_SG4 regions.
source: Vice versa, binding motifs for Tcf factors are enriched in the 257 mSTARR_Wnt regions when compared to mSTARR_SG4 regions (Figure 2K, Supplementary file 1-Supplementary Table 2A).
evidence: This is based on HOMER motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2K.

claim: 254 hSTARR-REs were identified by combining human STARR-seq regions activated by either SG4- or Tcf-factors throughout the TBX3 locus.
source: First, we combined the human STARR-seq regions activated by either SG4- or Tcf-factors throughout the TBX3 locus, resulting in 254 hSTARR-REs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 24 putative cardiac-specific hEMERGE REs were found within the TBX3 locus.
source: Second, although epigenomic data from human AVCS tissue is scarce, we used cardiac-specific EMERGE enhancer prediction (van Duijvenboden et al., 2016) and found 24 putative cardiac-specific hEMERGE REs within the TBX3 locus (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and based on EMERGE prediction.

claim: 62 mouse orthologous regions were identified by translating and mapping the genomic sequences of the 67 mATAC_AVJ regions to the human genome.
source: Third, we translated and mapped the genomic sequences of the 67 mATAC_AVJ regions and of the cardiac-specific mouse EMERGE predicted enhancers to the human genome, resulting in 62 mouse orthologous regions (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 296 candidate RE regions in the human TBX3 locus were identified by combining three approaches.
source: Combined, this approach resulted in 296 candidate RE regions in the human TBX3 locus, based on sequence activity (hSTARR), enhancer prediction based on various cardiac-specific epigenomic datasets (hEMERGE), and conservation with active and AVCS-specific accessible genomic regions from the mouse genome (mouse orthologous regions) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The previously identified human enhancer Tbx3-eA is marked by all three criteria (hSTARR, hEMERGE, and mouse orthologous).
source: The previously identified human enhancer Tbx3-eA, driving AVCS expression and responding to Smad/Gata stimulation in vitro (van Weerd et al., 2014), is marked by all three criteria, supporting the validity of our approach (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and validates the approach.

claim: Seven candidate variant REs were found within human VR1.
source: To assess whether these RE candidates harbor common variants associated with PR interval or QRS duration, we filtered for genomic location within VR1 or VR2 and found seven candidate variant REs within human VR1 and 13 candidate variant REs within VR2 (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1-Supplementary Table 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 13 candidate variant REs were found within VR2.
source: To assess whether these RE candidates harbor common variants associated with PR interval or QRS duration, we filtered for genomic location within VR1 or VR2 and found seven candidate variant REs within human VR1 and 13 candidate variant REs within VR2 (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1-Supplementary Table 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Six candidate REs in VR1 harbor one or multiple variants.
source: Combined, we found six candidate REs in VR1 and 6 candidate REs in VR2 harboring one or multiple variants (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Six candidate REs in VR2 harbor one or multiple variants.
source: Combined, we found six candidate REs in VR1 and 6 candidate REs in VR2 harboring one or multiple variants (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: All RE candidates except for hRE5 drove basal luciferase reporter activity in both HL-1 and COS-7 cells.
source: We measured luciferase reporter activity of the major and minor haplotype of these RE candidates and found that all RE candidates except for hRE5 drove basal luciferase reporter activity in both HL-1 and COS-7 cells (n = 4; p<0.05); hRE5 decreased reporter activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: hRE5 decreased reporter activity.
source: We measured luciferase reporter activity of the major and minor haplotype of these RE candidates and found that all RE candidates except for hRE5 drove basal luciferase reporter activity in both HL-1 and COS-7 cells (n = 4; p<0.05); hRE5 decreased reporter activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The risk allele of hRE5, hRE7, hRE8 and hRE18 increased basal reporter activity in HL-1 cells when compared to the reference allele.
source: The risk allele of 4 REs (hRE5, hRE7, hRE8 and hRE18) increased basal reporter activity in HL-1 cells when compared to the reference allele, whereas the risk allele of hRE9, hRE11 and hRE15-16 decreased basal reporter activity in both HL-1 and COS-7 cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The risk allele of hRE9, hRE11 and hRE15-16 decreased basal reporter activity in both HL-1 and COS-7 cells.
source: The risk allele of 4 REs (hRE5, hRE7, hRE8 and hRE18) increased basal reporter activity in HL-1 cells when compared to the reference allele, whereas the risk allele of hRE9, hRE11 and hRE15-16 decreased basal reporter activity in both HL-1 and COS-7 cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The risk allele of hRE3 and hRE9 increased SG4-dependent activity.
source: The SG4-dependent activity of hRE3 and hRE9 and the Wnt-dependent activity of hRE6 was increased by the risk allele, whereas the risk allele of hRE8, hRE15-16 and hRE18 decreased both SG4- and Wnt-dependent activity (hRE8, hRE18), or only Wnt-response (hRE15-16).
evidence: This is based on luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The risk allele of hRE6 increased Wnt-dependent activity.
source: The SG4-dependent activity of hRE3 and hRE9 and the Wnt-dependent activity of hRE6 was increased by the risk allele, whereas the risk allele of hRE8, hRE15-16 and hRE18 decreased both SG4- and Wnt-dependent activity (hRE8, hRE18), or only Wnt-response (hRE15-16).
evidence: This is based on luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The risk allele of hRE8 and hRE18 decreased both SG4- and Wnt-dependent activity.
source: The SG4-dependent activity of hRE3 and hRE9 and the Wnt-dependent activity of hRE6 was increased by the risk allele, whereas the risk allele of hRE8, hRE15-16 and hRE18 decreased both SG4- and Wnt-dependent activity (hRE8, hRE18), or only Wnt-response (hRE15-16).
evidence: This is based on luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The risk allele of hRE15-16 decreased only Wnt-response.
source: The SG4-dependent activity of hRE3 and hRE9 and the Wnt-dependent activity of hRE6 was increased by the risk allele, whereas the risk allele of hRE8, hRE15-16 and hRE18 decreased both SG4- and Wnt-dependent activity (hRE8, hRE18), or only Wnt-response (hRE15-16).
evidence: This is based on luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: None of the variants within the functionally affected fragments matched known TF binding motifs.
source: We next analyzed whether potential TF binding motifs were disrupted or de novo created by the respective SNP in the variant region of the functionally affected REs to elucidate, thereby possibly explaining the differential effect of the risk allele on luciferase activity. None of the variants within the functionally affected fragments matched known TF binding motifs.
evidence: This is based on motif analysis using JASPAR.

claim: The murine region homologous to human VR2 is located within a region that harbors sequences driving Tbx3 expression in the ventral, right-sided and dorsal aspect of the AV canal.
source: The murine region homologous to human VR2 is located within a region that we previously demonstrated to harbor sequences driving Tbx3 expression in the ventral, right-sided and dorsal (primordial AV node) aspect of the AV canal (BAC 366H17-GFP; −82 kb to +78 kb relative to Tbx3; Figure 5; van Weerd et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on previous work cited and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Sequences within VR1 and VR2 are to a large extent evolutionary conserved between human and mouse.
source: Sequences within VR1 and VR2 are to a large extent evolutionary conserved between human and mouse, and VR2 harbors the AVC-specific RE (Tbx3-eA) that was functionally and structurally conserved between mouse and human (van Weerd et al., 2014; Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A,B with conservation tracks and supported by citation.

claim: VR2 harbors the AVC-specific RE (Tbx3-eA) that was functionally and structurally conserved between mouse and human.
source: Sequences within VR1 and VR2 are to a large extent evolutionary conserved between human and mouse, and VR2 harbors the AVC-specific RE (Tbx3-eA) that was functionally and structurally conserved between mouse and human (van Weerd et al., 2014; Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Immunohistochemistry on sections of Tbx3-459M16-GFP E14.5 embryos revealed GFP reporter expression throughout the entire AVCS in a pattern resembling that of endogenous Tbx3.
source: Although this BAC does not overlap VR2 and does not contain the previously identified RE (Tbx3-eA) driving AV node expression (van Weerd et al., 2014), immunohistochemistry on sections of Tbx3-459M16-GFP E14.5 embryos revealed GFP reporter expression throughout the entire AVCS in a pattern resembling that of endogenous Tbx3, including the full AV canal and prospective AV node, AV bundle and BBs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C with immunohistochemistry data.

claim: 459M16-GFP expression was found in the eye, ear, genital tubercle, limbs, and mammary glands.
source: Furthermore, expression was found in the eye, ear, genital tubercle, limbs, and mammary glands (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Multiple physically separated regulatory regions independently drive AVCS expression.
source: These observations suggest that multiple physically separated regulatory regions independently drive AVCS expression (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is inferred from the BAC transgenic data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Tbx3+/+, Tbx3ΔVR1/+ and Tbx3ΔVR1/ΔVR1 mice were born according to Mendelian ratios.
source: Tbx3+/+, Tbx3ΔVR1/+ and Tbx3ΔVR1/ΔVR1 mice were born according to Mendelian ratios (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Expression of Tbx3, Med13l and Tbx5 was not affected in E13.5 Tbx3ΔVR1/ΔVR1 AV junctions.
source: We measured expression levels in microdissected AV junctions (containing the AV node and AV bundle) of E13.5 Tbx3+/+ and Tbx3ΔVR1/ΔVR1 hearts and found that expression of Tbx3 or neighboring Med13l and Tbx5 was not affected (Figure 6C, not shown for Med13l and Tbx5).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: No difference in PR interval or QRS duration was found between Tbx3+/+ and Tbx3ΔVR1/ΔVR1 adult mice by surface ECG.
source: To elucidate whether deletion of VR1 affects AVCS function postnatally, we performed surface ECGs on adult Tbx3+/+ and Tbx3ΔVR1/ΔVR1 mice and found no difference in PR interval or QRS duration between genotypes (Tbx3+/+ n = 10, Tbx3ΔVR1/+ n = 12, Tbx3ΔVR1/ΔVR1 n = 9; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is based on ECG data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: No difference in conduction parameters was found between Tbx3+/+ and Tbx3ΔVR1/ΔVR1 hearts by ex vivo ECG recordings on Langendorff perfused hearts.
source: To exclude a possible rescue effect of the sympathetic nervous system on AVCS function in the absence of VR1, we measured conduction parameters by ex vivo ECG recordings on Langendorff perfused hearts and again found no difference between Tbx3+/+ and Tbx3ΔVR1/ΔVR1 hearts (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is based on ex vivo ECG data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: The observed number of Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 pups postnatally was approximately half of the expected number.
source: Postnatally, however, the observed number of Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 pups was approximately half of the expected number (p=0.004, χ2 test; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D with statistical analysis.

claim: An approximately 2.5-fold increase in Tbx3 expression was found in Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 AV junctions compared to Tbx3+/+ littermates.
source: We analyzed expression levels of Tbx3 in microdissected AV junctions of E13.5 hearts and found an approximately 2.5-fold increase in expression in Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 hearts compared to Tbx3+/+ littermates (p=2*10−11; n = 8 and n = 9, respectively; Figure 6E), respectively.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 hearts showed increased expression of Hcn4 compared to wildtype littermates.
source: Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 hearts showed increased expression of Hcn4 (p=0.04) and Cacna1g (p=0.004), ion channel-encoding genes involved in AVCS function, and decreased expression of Scn5a (p=0.02), the cardiac sodium channel Nav1.5-encoding gene involved in conduction, compared to hearts of wildtype littermates (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 hearts showed increased expression of Cacna1g compared to wildtype littermates.
source: Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 hearts showed increased expression of Hcn4 (p=0.04) and Cacna1g (p=0.004), ion channel-encoding genes involved in AVCS function, and decreased expression of Scn5a (p=0.02), the cardiac sodium channel Nav1.5-encoding gene involved in conduction, compared to hearts of wildtype littermates (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 hearts showed decreased expression of Scn5a compared to wildtype littermates.
source: Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 hearts showed increased expression of Hcn4 (p=0.04) and Cacna1g (p=0.004), ion channel-encoding genes involved in AVCS function, and decreased expression of Scn5a (p=0.02), the cardiac sodium channel Nav1.5-encoding gene involved in conduction, compared to hearts of wildtype littermates (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Expression levels of Gja5 and Gja1 were not affected in Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 hearts.
source: Expression levels of Gja5 and Gja1, target genes of Tbx3 in the AVCS and encoding the fast conducting gap junction proteins Cx40 and Cx43, respectively, were not affected (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Expression of Tbx5, Rbm19 and Med13l was unchanged in Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 AV junctions.
source: To assess whether deletion of VR2 affects the expression of genes flanking Tbx3, we measured expression levels of Tbx5, Rbm19 and Med13l and found that expression of these genes was unchanged (Figure 6F), suggesting VR2 only regulates Tbx3 in the AVCS.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: VR2 only regulates Tbx3 in the AVCS.
source: To assess whether deletion of VR2 affects the expression of genes flanking Tbx3, we measured expression levels of Tbx5, Rbm19 and Med13l and found that expression of these genes was unchanged (Figure 6F), suggesting VR2 only regulates Tbx3 in the AVCS.
evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression data showing only Tbx3 is affected.

claim: Increased Tbx3 expression was found only in the SAN of Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 embryos, not in forelimbs, liver or lungs.
source: We measured Tbx3 expression levels in sinoatrial nodes (SANs), forelimbs, liver and lungs of E13.5 embryos, and found increased expression only in the SAN (p=0.013). Expression in other tissues was not affected (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: No difference in Tbx3 expression pattern was observed between Tbx3+/+ and Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 hearts by in situ hybridization.
source: We performed in situ hybridization on E13.5 Tbx3+/+ and Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 hearts and observed no difference in expression pattern for Tbx3 between Tbx3+/+ and Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 hearts (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6G with in situ hybridization data.

claim: Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 mice showed shortened PR intervals compared to Tbx3+/+ mice (30.4 ms vs 35.3 ms, p=0.025).
source: Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 mice showed shortened PR intervals compared to Tbx3+/+ mice (30.4 ms and 35.3 ms, respectively; p=0.025; Figure 6H, Figure 6—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is based on surface ECG data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The QRS duration in Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 mice was increased compared to wildtypes (15.1 ms vs 11.7 ms, p=0.004).
source: The QRS duration in Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 mice was increased compared to wildtypes (15.1 ms and 11.7 ms, respectively; p=0.004; Figure 6I, Figure 6—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is based on surface ECG data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Ex vivo ECG recordings on Langendorff perfused hearts revealed a similar effect on PR interval and QRS duration as in vivo recordings.
source: Recordings of ex vivo ECGs on these hearts under Langendorff perfusion revealed a similar effect on PR interval and QRS duration, suggesting the autonomic nervous system is not involved in changed parameters upon deletion of VR2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2G,H).
evidence: This is based on ex vivo ECG data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2G,H.

claim: The autonomic nervous system is not involved in the changed ECG parameters upon deletion of VR2.
source: Recordings of ex vivo ECGs on these hearts under Langendorff perfusion revealed a similar effect on PR interval and QRS duration, suggesting the autonomic nervous system is not involved in changed parameters upon deletion of VR2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2G,H).
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity between in vivo and ex vivo ECG results.

claim: Deletion of VR1 in mice does not affect expression levels or AVCS function.
source: Taken together, these results show that deletion of VR1 in mice does not affect expression levels or AVCS function.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the VR1 deletion data presented.

claim: Deletion of VR2 affects Tbx3 expression in the AVCS and causes misregulation of target genes and affected conduction parameters.
source: Deletion of VR2 affects Tbx3 expression in the AVCS and causes misregulation of target genes and affected conduction parameters.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the VR2 deletion data presented.

claim: Common GWAS variants typically have small effect sizes on traits.
source: GWAS typically identifies common variants, relatively frequently present in the human genome, and their effect size on the respective traits is usually small (Manolio et al., 2009; McCarthy et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to GWAS literature.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of TBX3, TBX5 and other transcription factor-encoding genes causes congenital defects.
source: Haploinsufficiency of TBX3, TBX5 and other transcription factor-encoding genes causes congenital defects (Bamshad et al., 1997; Basson et al., 1999; Seidman and Seidman, 2002) and is therefore not well tolerated, implying that even the modest effects of common variants on expression of such genes may have a relatively large effect on phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical genetics literature.

claim: The cardiac and limb expression of Tbx3 involves multiple redundant or synergistically acting REs.
source: The cardiac and limb expression of Tbx3 involves multiple redundant or synergistically acting REs, which was previously shown by modified BAC and reporter transgenics (Osterwalder et al., 2018; van Weerd et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Associations for many disease risk loci arise from multiple variants in LD that affect clusters of enhancers targeting the same gene.
source: Indeed, associations for many disease risk loci arise from multiple variants in LD that affect clusters of enhancers targeting the same gene (Corradin and Scacheri, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The two TBX3 risk loci harbor multiple active REs whose activity is affected by their respective risk alleles.
source: Therefore, we set out to assess the effect of deletion of the entire variant regions within the TBX3 locus rather than assessing the effect of individual SNPs, and found that the two TBX3 risk loci harbor multiple active REs whose activity is affected by their respective risk alleles.
evidence: This is based on the luciferase assay data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Common genomic variation within VR1 and VR2 probably affects the function of multiple redundant REs that together orchestrate the complex regulation of Tbx3 expression in the AVCS.
source: Common genomic variation within these regions therefore probably affects the function of multiple redundant REs, rather than individual elements, that together orchestrate the complex regulation of Tbx3 expression in the AVCS.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing multiple REs are affected by variants.

claim: Disease-causing non-coding variants in the human genome can affect RE activity and thereby gene expression by altering transcription factor binding.
source: Disease-causing non-coding variants in the human genome can affect RE activity and thereby gene expression by altering transcription factor binding (Deplancke et al., 2016; Maurano et al., 2012; Schaub et al., 2012), resulting in GWAS association.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Genomic deletion of the entire VR1 removes the potentially affected REs from the genome and disrupts the topology of the locus.
source: Genomic deletion of the entire VR1 removes the potentially affected REs from the genome and disrupts the topology of the locus, which could be functionally buffered by redundancy within the locus (Cannavò et al., 2016; Long et al., 2016; Osterwalder et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the deletion strategy and supported by citations.

claim: Regulatory redundancy could be deployed in the case of genomic deletion but not in the case of only a variable nucleotide in an otherwise unaffected regulatory sequence.
source: Such redundancy is possibly not deployed in the case of only a variable nucleotide in an otherwise unaffected regulatory sequence (or genomic topology), providing a possible explanation for the absence of effect we observed in Tbx3∆VR1/∆VR1 mice (Cannavò et al., 2016; Long et al., 2016; Osterwalder et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation to explain the lack of phenotype in VR1 deletion mice.

claim: The increased expression of Tbx3 in Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 hearts could be caused by a disruption of the fine balance between activating and repressive REs within VR2.
source: As we have previously identified an RE (Tbx3-eA) that activates gene expression in the AVCS (van Weerd et al., 2014) that is located within VR2 (van Weerd et al., 2014), the increased expression of Tbx3 observed in Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 hearts could be caused by a disruption of the fine balance between activating and repressive REs within VR2 that orchestrate the modulation of Tbx3 regulation.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the increased Tbx3 expression upon VR2 deletion.

claim: Multiple regions within VR2 are marked by H3K27me3 in the adult heart.
source: Indeed, in the adult heart multiple regions within VR2 are marked by H3K27me3 (data not shown), a histone mark associated with transcriptional repression (Gilsbach et al., 2014; Mozzetta et al., 2015), suggesting VR2 potentially harbors multiple silencer elements.
evidence: This is stated but the data is not shown in the manuscript.

claim: VR2 potentially harbors multiple silencer elements.
source: Indeed, in the adult heart multiple regions within VR2 are marked by H3K27me3 (data not shown), a histone mark associated with transcriptional repression (Gilsbach et al., 2014; Mozzetta et al., 2015), suggesting VR2 potentially harbors multiple silencer elements.
evidence: This is inferred from the H3K27me3 marks and supported by citations.

claim: Tbx3 has a large number of target genes enriched for ion handling protein-encoding genes.
source: Tbx3 has a large number of target genes enriched for ion handling protein-encoding genes (Bakker et al., 2012; Frank et al., 2011; Horsthuis et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hundreds of genes that potentially influence the electrophysiological properties of the AVCS are likely to be deregulated in Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2.
source: As such, hundreds of genes that potentially influence the electrophysiological properties of the AVCS are likely to be deregulated in Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2.
evidence: This is inferred from the known role of Tbx3 in regulating many target genes.

claim: Proper AVCS function depends on strictly balanced Tbx3 levels.
source: Not only Tbx3 insufficiency (Bakker et al., 2008; Frank et al., 2011; Horsthuis et al., 2009) but also over-expression (this study, Burnicka-Turek et al., 2020) can be detrimental, suggesting proper AVCS function depends on strictly balanced Tbx3 levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the current study and supported by citations.

claim: The balance between Tbx3 and Tbx5 was found to be important in the function and gene regulation of the VCS.
source: The balance between Tbx3 (imposing a nodal gene program) and Tbx5 (imposing a fast-conductive gene program) was found to be important in the function and gene regulation of the VCS (i.e. AV bundle and branches) (Burnicka-Turek et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The Tbx3/Tbx5 balance model does not hold for the AV node.
source: This balance model would predict conduction slowing when Tbx3 levels are increased. However, we observed shortened PR intervals indicative of faster AVCS conduction in Tbx3∆VR2/∆VR2 mice (which have 2–3 fold increased Tbx3 expression levels in AVCS), while Tbx5 was not deregulated. This suggests that the Tbx3/Tbx5 balance model does not hold for the AV node.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that increased Tbx3 led to faster conduction rather than slower.

claim: A major limitation of STARR-seq is that DNA fragments are tested for regulatory potential episomally and out of genomic context.
source: A major limitation of massive parallel reporter assays like STARR-seq is that DNA fragments are tested for regulatory potential episomally and out of genomic context (Arnold et al., 2013), lacking the intricate relationship between DNA, histones and long range chromatin interactions (Gallagher and Chen-Plotkin, 2018; Inoue and Ahituv, 2015).
evidence: This is a known limitation of the method supported by citations.

claim: STARR-seq potentially yields multiple false positive sequences that are transcriptionally active but not relevant for endogenous gene regulation.
source: Intrinsic sequence activity or transcription factor binding to motifs within regions endogenously repressed or residing in closed chromatin might activate reporter gene expression when tested in episomal assays. This potentially yields multiple false positive sequences, that is transcriptionally active sequences not relevant for endogenous gene regulation (Inukai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a known limitation of the method supported by citation.

claim: The bacterial plasmid origin-of-replication within the STARR-seq vector acts as a conflicting core-promoter, causing confounding false-positives and negatives.
source: Furthermore, we used the reporter vector described in Arnold et al., 2013 to generate our libraries. A recent study from the same group showed that the bacterial plasmid origin-of-replication within this vector acts as a conflicting core-promoter, thereby causing confounding false-positives and –negatives (Muerdter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a limitation of the specific vector used, supported by citation.

claim: The relatively high basal activity of the super core promoter (SCP1) in the STARR-seq vector potentially decreases the fold-change of signal to input.
source: In addition, the relatively high basal activity of the super core promoter (SCP1) in this vector potentially decreases the fold-change of signal to input (Muerdter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a limitation of the specific vector used, supported by citation.

claim: Enhancer activity often depends on its ability to interact with the proper promoter.
source: As enhancer activity often depends on its ability to interact with the proper promoter (Arnold et al., 2017; Zabidi et al., 2015), testing our libraries with the endogenous Tbx3 promoter could yield more relevant RE candidates.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The weak overlap of STARR-seq regions with EMERGE and AVCS-ATAC-seq regions illustrates that a subset of the STARR-seq-identified active regions might not be transcriptionally relevant for Tbx3 expression in vivo.
source: The weak overlap of STARR-seq regions with EMERGE and AVCS-ATAC-seq regions illustrates that a subset of the STARR-seq-identified active regions might not be transcriptionally relevant for Tbx3 expression in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the overlap analysis presented in the results.

claim: The correlation is low between luciferase reporter activity and STARR-seq activity of candidate sequences from the murine genome.
source: Indeed, the correlation is low between luciferase reporter activity and STARR-seq activity of candidate sequences from the murine genome selected based on either strong epigenomic hallmarks (EMERGE/ChIP-seq/ATAC-seq; high luciferase-/low STARR-seq activity) or strong STARR-seq signal (mSTARR_SG4; high STARR-seq-/low luciferase activity) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: STARR-seq on the human TBX3 locus provides a useful albeit somewhat more supportive tool to identify REs given the scarcity of alternative epigenomic datasets derived from human AVCS tissue.
source: Nevertheless, given the scarcity of alternative epigenomic datasets derived from human AVCS tissue, STARR-seq on the human TBX3 locus provides a useful albeit somewhat more supportive tool to identify REs.
evidence: This is the authors' assessment of the utility of their approach.

claim: The high transfection efficiency of COS-7 cells allowed screening of multiple libraries on a large scale with sufficient coverage.
source: Although seemingly irrelevant for assessing regulatory activity of potential AVCS-involved REs, the high transfection efficiency of COS-7 cells allowed us to screen multiple libraries on a large scale and acquire sufficient coverage.
evidence: This justifies the use of COS-7 cells for STARR-seq.

claim: The inactivity of a cardiac-specific gene program in COS-7 cells allowed specific assessment of the response of genomic fragments to the cotransfected SG4- and Tcf-factors.
source: The inactivity of a cardiac-specific gene program in COS-7 cells furthermore allowed us to specifically assess the response of genomic fragments to the cotransfected SG4- and Tcf-factors.
evidence: This justifies the use of COS-7 cells for STARR-seq.

claim: Binding motifs for Smad/Gata and Tcf factors are specifically enriched in AVCS cardiomyocytes.
source: Our observation that binding motifs for these factors are specifically enriched in AVCS cardiomyocytes, indicated these factors may be involved in regulation of the AVCS gene program.
evidence: This is based on the motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Motif databases have limitations as they are incomplete and possibly inaccurate.
source: Motif enrichment in AVCS-specific accessible regions was performed by matching AVCS-specific accessible regions to motifs present in the HOMER database. Such databases have their limitations, as they are incomplete and possibly inaccurate as they derive their input from experimental procedures that are condition- and cell type-dependent.
evidence: This is a known limitation of motif analysis databases.

claim: The observed motif enrichment supported previous studies implicating Bmp-signalling (Smads), Gata4/6 and Wnt-signalling (Tcf) in AVCS patterning.
source: Nevertheless, the observed enrichment supported previous studies implicating Bmp-signalling (Smads), Gata4/6 and Wnt-signalling (Tcf) in AVCS patterning (Stefanovic et al., 2014; Gillers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: By focusing on SG4- and Wnt-responsive REs, a proportion of relevant sequences involved in the regulation of Tbx3 expression may be overlooked.
source: By focusing on SG4- and Wnt-responsive REs, we potentially overlook a proportion of relevant sequences involved in the regulation of Tbx3 expression, as multiple other factors are involved in AVCS development (Bhattacharyya and Munshi, 2020; Park and Fishman, 2017; van Eif et al., 2019).
evidence: This is acknowledged as a limitation and supported by citations.

claim: Recent advances in the generation of nodal-like cells derived from human pluripotent stem cells will provide a promising tool to study the regulation of genes involved in AVCS development.
source: Recent and ongoing advantages in the generation of (sinoatrial/atrioventricular) nodal-like cells derived from human pluripotent stem cells (Birket et al., 2015; Jung et al., 2014; Protze et al., 2017; Rimmbach et al., 2015) will provide a promising tool to study the regulation of genes involved in AVCS development and the function of candidate REs in a considerably more relevant cell type.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies on stem cell-derived cardiac cells.
